promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Wave properties and the wave equation

questions.q: Which equation correctly links wave speed, frequency and wavelength?
questions.explain: The wave equation states v = f λ, so wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of frequency?
questions.explain: Frequency is measured in hertz, where one hertz equals one wave (cycle) per second.

questions.q: Sound waves travelling through air are best described as:
questions.explain: Sound is a longitudinal wave in which the air oscillates parallel to the direction of energy transfer, forming compressions and rarefactions.

questions.q: The amplitude of a wave is:
options: The maximum displacement of a point from its rest position
The distance between two adjacent wave peaks
The number of waves passing a point each second
The time taken for one complete wave
questions.explain: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed (rest) position.

questions.q: The normal range of human hearing is approximately:
questions.explain: Humans can typically hear sounds with frequencies from about 20 Hz up to about 20,000 Hz (20 kHz).

questions.q: Ultrasound is sound with a frequency:
questions.explain: Ultrasound has frequencies above 20,000 Hz, which is greater than the upper limit of normal human hearing.

questions.q: When measuring the angle of incidence of a ray at a surface, the angle is measured between the ray and:
questions.explain: Angles of incidence and reflection are always measured from the normal, the line drawn at 90° to the surface at the point where the ray meets it.

questions.q: The wavelength of a wave is:
options: The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave
The maximum displacement from the rest position
The number of complete waves per second
The height of a wave crest above the trough
questions.explain: Wavelength is the distance between two adjacent identical points on a wave, for example crest to crest.

questions.q: What do all waves transfer as they travel?
options: Both matter and energy over long distances
questions.explain: Waves transfer energy (and information) from place to place without transferring the matter of the medium.

questions.q: In a transverse wave, the oscillations are:
options: Perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
Parallel to the direction of energy transfer
In the same direction as the wave's travel
questions.explain: In a transverse wave the particles oscillate at right angles to the direction in which the wave carries energy.

questions.q: A longitudinal wave consists of a series of:
questions.explain: In a longitudinal wave the medium is squeezed together and stretched apart, producing compressions and rarefactions along the direction of travel.

questions.q: According to the law of reflection, when a ray reflects from a plane mirror:
options: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
The angle of incidence is twice the angle of reflection
The reflected ray travels along the surface
The angle of reflection is always 90°
questions.explain: For reflection at a plane surface, the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

questions.q: Refraction of a wave at a boundary is caused by:
options: A change in the speed of the wave
A change in the frequency of the wave
The wave reflecting back on itself
questions.explain: Refraction occurs because the wave changes speed as it passes from one medium into another, which can change its direction.

questions.q: A ray of light passes from air into a glass block, where it travels more slowly. At the boundary the ray bends:
options: Along the surface of the glass
questions.explain: When light slows down entering a denser medium such as glass, it refracts towards the normal.

questions.q: Why can sound not travel through a vacuum?
options: There are no particles to vibrate and carry the wave
There is no light to carry the sound
questions.explain: Sound needs a medium of particles to vibrate; in a vacuum there are no particles, so the wave cannot be transmitted.

questions.q: If a wave has a frequency of 4 Hz, what is its period?
questions.explain: Period is the reciprocal of frequency, so T = 1/f = 1/4 = 0.25 s.

questions.q: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. What is its speed?
questions.explain: Using v = f λ = 50 × 2 = 100 m/s.

questions.q: A sound wave travels at 340 m/s and has a wavelength of 1.7 m. What is its frequency?
questions.explain: Rearranging v = f λ gives f = v/λ = 340 ÷ 1.7 = 200 Hz.

questions.q: A sound wave travels at 330 m/s with a frequency of 550 Hz. What is its wavelength?
questions.explain: Rearranging v = f λ gives λ = v/f = 330 ÷ 550 = 0.6 m.

questions.q: A ship sends an ultrasound pulse to the seabed. The echo returns after 0.5 s and sound travels at 1500 m/s in water. How deep is the seabed?
questions.explain: Total distance = speed × time = 1500 × 0.5 = 750 m; the seabed depth is half of this (there and back), so 375 m.
